title: DripDrop vs Liquid I.V.: Which Hydrates Better After Drinking?
excerpt: DripDrop vs Liquid I.V. compared: sodium, sugar, and water per stick, which works better for a hangover or nausea, how many to drink, and who should be careful.
metaDescription: DripDrop vs Liquid I.V.: sodium, sugar, and serving size compared, which is better for a hangover or nausea, and who should check with a doctor first.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** DripDrop and Liquid I.V. are built on the same science, but they're aimed at different jobs. DripDrop is a medical-style oral rehydration solution (ORS): it's mixed into a small amount of water, so each sip is saltier and more concentrated, and it's designed for real dehydration from vomiting, diarrhea, heat, or illness. Liquid I.V. is a wellness hydration mix: it's diluted in twice as much water, tastes more like a sports drink, and adds vitamins. If you're genuinely dried out, nauseous, or can only manage small sips, DripDrop is the better tool. If you're mildly thirsty and just want something pleasant that you'll actually finish, Liquid I.V. is fine. Neither one cures a hangover, because dehydration is only one piece of why you feel bad.

**The quick picks:**

- **Vomited, have diarrhea, or feel properly dried out:** DripDrop ORS, sipped slowly.
- **Mild hangover, mostly thirst and a dull headache:** either works. Liquid I.V. is easier to drink in a big glass.
- **Watching sugar:** both brands sell zero-sugar versions, but those give up some of the absorption benefit (explained below).
- **High blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or told to limit salt:** ask your doctor before using either regularly. Both carry a real sodium load.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Get medical help instead of reaching for an electrolyte drink if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle. If someone who drank heavily is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that may be alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

## DripDrop vs Liquid I.V. at a Glance

Both products change their formulas and flavors from time to time, so treat these as approximate figures for the standard versions and check your own box. The important column is the last one, because the two are mixed with very different amounts of water.

| | DripDrop ORS | Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Oral rehydration solution, marketed for dehydration | Hydration drink mix, marketed for everyday wellness |
| Water per stick | About 8 fl oz (roughly 240 ml) | About 16 fl oz (roughly 500 ml) |
| Sodium per stick | Around 330 mg | Around 500 mg |
| Potassium per stick | Around 185 mg | Around 370 mg |
| Sugar per stick | Around 7 to 8 g | Around 11 g |
| Added vitamins | Some versions add zinc and vitamin C | Vitamin C plus several B vitamins |
| Taste | Saltier, more "medicinal" | Sweeter, closer to a sports drink |
| Sodium per liter, as mixed | Roughly 1,300 to 1,400 mg | Roughly 1,000 mg |

That last row is the one most comparison pages skip. Per stick, Liquid I.V. looks like it has more sodium and more potassium. But you mix a DripDrop stick into half as much water, so **the drink you actually sip from DripDrop is more concentrated in sodium**. That's the whole point of an ORS, and it's why DripDrop tastes noticeably saltier.

## The Science They Share: Why Salt Plus Sugar Beats Plain Water

Both brands are based on the same idea, which has been used in medicine for decades. Your small intestine has a transporter that pulls sodium and glucose across the gut wall together. Water follows them. So a drink with the right balance of sodium and a little glucose is absorbed and held onto more efficiently than plain water, especially when you're losing fluid.

That idea is the basis of oral rehydration solution, which the World Health Organization and UNICEF promote for treating dehydration from diarrheal illness. It's one of the best-supported treatments in public health, and it's the reason a rehydration drink isn't just "fancy salt water."

The balance matters, though:

- **Too little sodium** and the drink acts much like plain water.
- **Too much sugar** pulls water *into* the gut instead of out of it, which can make diarrhea worse and slow rehydration. This is why the WHO moved to a lower-sugar, lower-concentration formula in the early 2000s.
- **Too much sodium** without enough water can be hard on people with heart or kidney problems and doesn't taste good enough to drink in quantity.

DripDrop is designed to sit closer to the medical end of that balance. Liquid I.V. leans toward the consumer end: a little less sodium per sip, a little more sweetness, and enough flavor that people drink it for fun.

### Where each sits next to the WHO formula

The WHO's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration salts contain about 75 mmol of sodium per liter, which works out to roughly 1,700 mg of sodium per liter, and about 13.5 g of glucose per liter. Using the approximate label figures above:

- **DripDrop** lands somewhat below the WHO sodium level and has more sugar per liter.
- **Liquid I.V.** lands further below the WHO sodium level, also with more sugar per liter than the WHO formula.

Neither is identical to the hospital formula, and that's fine for a typical hangover. The takeaway is that DripDrop is closer to a medical ORS on sodium, while both are sweeter than the WHO version. If you ever have severe diarrhea or vomiting that lasts, pharmacy ORS products and medical advice are the right step, not a branded drink mix.

## DripDrop: Pros and Cons

DripDrop was created by a physician to treat dehydration and markets itself as a medical-grade oral rehydration solution. Its main product comes as powder sticks you mix into about 8 ounces of water. The company also sells versions with no sugar and larger-serving formats, so check which one you're buying.

**What it does well:**

- **Concentrated rehydration in a small volume.** When you feel queasy, a full 16-ounce glass can feel impossible. An 8-ounce serving sipped over 20 to 30 minutes is much easier to keep down.
- **Higher sodium per sip.** That's what you want after vomiting, diarrhea, or a hot day with a lot of sweating on top of drinking.
- **Built for illness, not just wellness.** It's a reasonable thing to keep in a medicine cabinet for stomach bugs too.
- **Less sugar per stick** than Liquid I.V., though, as noted above, not necessarily less per liter.

**Where it falls short:**

- **Taste.** It's saltier, and plenty of people find it less pleasant. A rehydration drink you leave half-finished isn't doing much.
- **Small serving.** If you're only mildly dehydrated, 8 ounces doesn't add much fluid on its own. You'll want plain water alongside it.
- **Not a hangover cure.** It fixes fluid and salt loss. That's all it's designed to do.
- **Easier to find online** than in some stores, depending on where you live.

## Liquid I.V.: Pros and Cons

Liquid I.V.'s main product is the Hydration Multiplier, a powder stick mixed into 16 ounces of water. The brand calls its formula "Cellular Transport Technology," which is a marketing name for the same sodium-and-glucose principle behind ORS. It also sells Sugar-Free, Energy (with caffeine), and Sleep (with melatonin and other ingredients) lines. For a deeper look at the brand on its own, see our full guide to [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover).

**What it does well:**

- **Taste and drinkability.** Most people find it easier to drink, and a drink you finish beats a better formula you don't.
- **More total fluid.** The serving is 16 ounces, so you're getting twice the water with each stick.
- **More potassium per stick.** Useful if you're low after a night of peeing a lot, though most people get plenty from food.
- **Easy to find.** It's sold in most big grocery stores, pharmacies, and warehouse clubs.

**Where it falls short:**

- **More sugar per stick.** Around 11 g isn't a lot compared with a soda, but it adds up if you have several a day or you're watching blood sugar.
- **Less sodium per sip.** Fine for mild dehydration, a bit weak if you've been sick.
- **The vitamins don't do much for a hangover.** There's no good evidence that a dose of B vitamins and vitamin C changes how a hangover feels in people who eat a normal diet.
- **Some versions are a bad fit after drinking.** More on the Energy and Sleep lines below.

## Which Is Better for a Hangover?

It depends on what kind of hangover you have. Here's the honest breakdown.

| Your morning | Better pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Thirsty, dry mouth, mild headache | Either; Liquid I.V. is easier | Mild dehydration. Total fluid matters more than the exact formula. |
| Dark urine, dizzy when you stand up | DripDrop, plus water | Real fluid and sodium loss. A more concentrated ORS helps most. |
| Nauseous or you've vomited | DripDrop, in small sips | Small, frequent sips of ORS are the standard way to keep fluids down. |
| Diarrhea after drinking | DripDrop | Ongoing fluid and salt loss is exactly what ORS is for. |
| You just want something tasty while you recover | Liquid I.V. | Fine. You'll drink more of it. |
| You avoid sugar | Either brand's zero-sugar version, or LMNT | Works for taste and salts, but loses some absorption benefit. |

### The part both brands' marketing skips

When researchers have measured hydration markers and electrolytes in hungover volunteers, they've generally found only a weak link between how dehydrated people were and how bad their hangover felt. Dehydration is real after heavy drinking, and fixing it helps the thirst, the dry mouth, and the lightheaded feeling. But the bigger drivers of a hangover are other things: **acetaldehyde** (the toxic compound your liver makes from alcohol), **inflammation**, **broken sleep**, and an **irritated stomach**.

No electrolyte drink touches those. That's why you can drink a liter of water before bed and still wake up rough. So whichever you choose, expect "somewhat better," not "fixed." There is no good evidence that DripDrop, Liquid I.V., or any electrolyte drink prevents or shortens a hangover on its own. If nausea is your main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps beyond fluids.

## How to Use Either One After Drinking

The method matters more than the brand.

1. **Before bed:** if you can, have one serving and a glass of water before you sleep. You're starting the night with fluid on board instead of waking up already behind.
2. **In the morning:** one serving, then plain water through the morning. Thirst and the color of your urine are reasonable guides. Pale yellow is the goal.
3. **If you're nauseous:** sip, don't gulp. A few mouthfuls every few minutes is better than a big glass that comes back up. This is where DripDrop's small serving shines.
4. **Eat when you can.** Food brings more sodium, potassium, and sugar on its own. Toast, bananas, eggs, broth, or a salty breakfast all help. See our [hangover breakfast guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) for ideas.
5. **Don't stack sticks.** One or two servings over a hangover morning is plenty for most people. Taking four or five puts a lot of sodium in your body for no extra benefit.

Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing in more detail.

## How Many Sticks a Day Is Too Many?

Both brands label their products for daily use, and for healthy adults one or two servings a day is generally fine. The issue is sodium. Most adults already get more sodium from food than health guidelines recommend, and US guidelines suggest keeping it under about 2,300 mg a day for most people.

- Two Liquid I.V. sticks add around 1,000 mg of sodium.
- Two DripDrop sticks add around 660 mg of sodium (but in much less water).

That's fine as a one-off after a night out, especially if you've been sweating or sick. It's not a great daily habit for most people who aren't losing fluid. **If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or you take medicines that affect sodium or potassium** (some blood pressure pills and water pills, for example), talk to your doctor before using either product regularly.

## Sugar vs Zero-Sugar Versions

Both brands sell sugar-free lines, and it's a fair question whether they're better.

The trade-off is simple. The glucose in the regular versions isn't just for taste. It's part of how the drink pulls water into your body. Zero-sugar versions keep the salts and the flavor but use sweeteners (such as allulose or stevia, depending on the product) that don't work the same way in the gut's sodium-glucose transporter. You still get the electrolytes and the water, which is helpful. You just lose some of the speed advantage.

For a typical hangover, a zero-sugar version is fine if that's what you prefer. If you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, the regular sugar version, or a proper pharmacy ORS, is the better pick. People with diabetes should talk to their doctor about which rehydration option suits them.

## What About the Energy and Sleep Versions?

This is where the brands differ more than people realize, mainly on Liquid I.V.'s side.

- **Liquid I.V. Energy** contains caffeine. A little caffeine the morning after can help if you're a regular coffee drinker and would otherwise get a withdrawal headache. But caffeine can also worsen nausea, a racing heart, and anxiety, all common after heavy drinking. Skip it if you're already jittery. And don't mix caffeine with alcohol on the night itself, since it can make you feel less drunk than you are. Our guide on [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains why that combination is worth avoiding.
- **Liquid I.V. Sleep** contains melatonin and other sleep ingredients. Don't take it with alcohol in your system. Alcohol is already a sedative, and stacking sleep aids on top of it isn't a good idea. See our guide on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) for the details.
- **DripDrop** is mostly sold as a straight rehydration product, so this issue comes up less. Still, read the label of any flavor or variant you buy.

## DripDrop vs Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte

People searching this comparison often have Pedialyte in mind too. Pedialyte is the other big medical-style ORS. Its classic ready-to-drink formula is similar in spirit to DripDrop: moderate sodium, some potassium, and a small amount of sugar, designed for illness rather than wellness.

- **DripDrop vs Pedialyte:** very similar job. DripDrop is a powder that packs small; classic Pedialyte comes ready to drink, and Pedialyte also sells powders and higher-electrolyte versions. Pick on taste, format, and price.
- **Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte:** Liquid I.V. is the sweeter, lighter, more pleasant option. Pedialyte is the better tool when you've actually been sick.

Our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) and the wider [electrolyte drinks compared guide](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) put all the main options side by side, including LMNT, Nuun, Gatorade, and Electrolit. For other head-to-heads, see [Liquid I.V. vs Gatorade](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-gatorade), [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv), [Instant Hydration vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/instant-hydration-vs-liquid-iv), [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte), or make your own with our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) recipe.

## Price and Convenience

Prices change too often to quote reliably, and both brands sell in packs of different sizes, so compare the cost per stick at your store. In general, both are much more expensive than a store-brand oral rehydration solution, which does the same core job. If cost matters, a pharmacy's own-brand ORS powder is a perfectly good substitute for either.

For travel, both come as flat powder sticks that fit in a bag. DripDrop's smaller serving is handy when you only have a small bottle. Liquid I.V. is easier to find on the go because it's stocked in more mainstream stores.

## Who Should Be Careful With Either

You should check with a doctor or pharmacist before using DripDrop or Liquid I.V. regularly if you:

- Have **high blood pressure** or have been told to limit salt
- Have **kidney disease** or **heart failure**
- Have **diabetes** (mainly for the sugar versions)
- Take **medicines that affect potassium or sodium**, such as some blood pressure pills (ACE inhibitors and ARBs), potassium-sparing water pills, or lithium
- Are pregnant and have been given specific fluid or salt advice

For children, follow the product's own age guidance and ask a pediatrician. This article is about adults recovering from drinking.

## When Dehydration Isn't the Real Problem

An electrolyte drink helps a normal hangover a little. It can't handle a medical problem. Get help if:

- You can't keep any fluids down for several hours, or you're vomiting repeatedly
- There's blood in your vomit or stool, or your vomit looks like coffee grounds
- You've barely urinated in 8 hours or more
- You feel faint, confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle
- Symptoms are getting worse instead of better by the afternoon

If someone who drank heavily is confused, hard to wake, having seizures, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that may be [alcohol poisoning](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs), not a hangover. Call 911 right away and don't leave them alone. No drink mix is a substitute for emergency care.

## Where DHM Fits In

Electrolyte drinks deal with fluid loss. They don't do anything about how your body handles the alcohol itself. That's the gap some people try to fill with **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver.

To be straight about the evidence: most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace water, food, sleep, or simply drinking less. If you want to try it, take it with plenty of water on the night you drink. Popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [best DHM supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) compares the main brands.

The habits with the best evidence are still the boring ones: pace yourself, alternate alcohol with water, eat before and while you drink, and get a full night's sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers them in detail.

## The Bottom Line

- **DripDrop** is a medical-style oral rehydration solution: saltier per sip, smaller serving, best when you're genuinely dehydrated, nauseous, or have been sick.
- **Liquid I.V.** is a wellness hydration mix: more water per stick, sweeter, easier to drink, and fine for mild dehydration.
- Per stick, Liquid I.V. has more sodium and sugar. Per sip, DripDrop is more concentrated in sodium, because it's mixed in half the water.
- Neither cures a hangover. They help the dehydration piece, which is real but usually not the main reason you feel bad.
- One or two servings after a night out is plenty. Talk to a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart disease, diabetes, or take medicines that affect sodium or potassium.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is DripDrop better than Liquid I.V.?**

For real dehydration, yes. DripDrop is built as an oral rehydration solution and is mixed into about 8 ounces of water, so each sip has more sodium than Liquid I.V. mixed in 16 ounces. That makes it the better tool after vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating. For mild thirst, Liquid I.V. is just as useful and easier to drink, and a drink you'll finish matters more than small formula differences.

**Which is better for a hangover, DripDrop or Liquid I.V.?**

If your hangover comes with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dizziness when you stand, DripDrop sipped slowly is the better pick. If you mostly feel thirsty with a mild headache, either works, and Liquid I.V. is more pleasant. Neither cures a hangover. They help with dehydration, which is only one part of why you feel bad.

**Does DripDrop or Liquid I.V. have more sodium?**

Per stick, Liquid I.V. has more, around 500 mg versus around 330 mg for DripDrop ORS. But DripDrop is mixed into half as much water, so the drink you sip is more concentrated: roughly 1,300 to 1,400 mg of sodium per liter for DripDrop versus roughly 1,000 mg per liter for Liquid I.V. Figures vary by version, so check your box.

**Which has more sugar, DripDrop or Liquid I.V.?**

Liquid I.V. has more sugar per stick, around 11 g, compared with around 7 to 8 g for DripDrop ORS. Because DripDrop uses less water, the sugar per liter is actually similar or a bit higher. Both brands also sell zero-sugar versions, which keep the salts but lose some of the absorption benefit that comes from glucose.

**Can I drink DripDrop or Liquid I.V. every day?**

Most healthy adults can have one or two servings a day, but daily use adds a meaningful amount of sodium on top of what you already get from food, and it's not needed if you aren't losing fluid. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or take medicines that affect sodium or potassium, ask your doctor before using either regularly.

**Is DripDrop the same as Pedialyte?**

They do the same job. Both are medical-style oral rehydration solutions with moderate sodium, some potassium, and a small amount of sugar. DripDrop mainly comes as a powder you mix into a small amount of water, while classic Pedialyte is sold ready to drink as well as in powder form. Choose on taste, format, and price.

**Should I drink an electrolyte drink before bed after drinking?**

It's a reasonable habit. One serving plus a glass of water before sleep means you start the night with fluid on board. It won't prevent a hangover, because dehydration isn't the main cause, but it can make the thirst, dry mouth, and dehydration headache less severe in the morning. Avoid caffeinated or sleep-aid versions when alcohol is still in your system.
